content: The retreatment of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) aims to achieve two primary objectives. First, it seeks to meet the treatment target of 90% viral suppression among all individuals receiving first-line antiretroviral therapy (ART) by 2020. Second, it addresses the first strategic goal of the World Health Organization (WHO) Global Action Plan on HIV Drug Resistance (2017–2021), which focuses on the prevention and response to HIVDR. The 2017 WHO report on HIVDR highlights an increasing prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs, with higher rates observed in more recent studies across all WHO regions. The annual rise in NNRTI resistance was most pronounced in Eastern Africa and least significant in Asia. Nationally representative surveys conducted between 2014 and 2016 in 11 lowand middle-income countries revealed a high prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to efavirenz (EFV) or nevirapine (NVP), the most commonly used antiretroviral (ARV) drugs in these regions. In six countries—Argentina, Guatemala, Namibia, Nicaragua, Uganda, and Zimbabwe—the prevalence reached or exceeded 10%. The prevalence of NNRTI resistance observed in national HIVDR surveys aligns with other available data, including findings from a small sample of recently infected individuals enrolled in the Population-based HIV Impact Assessments surveys. A subanalysis of studies conducted between 2014 and 2016 showed NNRTI resistance prevalence near or above 10% in Eastern Africa, Southern Africa, and Latin America. Pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs was significantly higher among individuals initiating first-line ART with prior ARV drug exposure (e.g., women exposed to ARVs for prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) or individuals restarting ART after treatment interruption) compared to ARV drug-naïve ART initiators across all WHO regions. Seven national surveys monitoring pretreatment HIVDR in Africa, South America, and Asia reported similar findings regarding resistance in these two groups. To address the high prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs and its impact on treatment outcomes, WHO has strengthened its response through updated guidelines and broader efforts outlined in the Global Action Plan on HIV Drug Resistance. The 2016 WHO consolidated ARV guidelines recommend an NNRTI-based regimen for individuals initiating or reinitiating first-line ART, except for children under three years of age. For this group, regimens containing ritonavir-boosted protease inhibitors (PI/r) are preferred due to the high rates of resistance associated with NNRTI exposure for PMTCT and other considerations. Most lowand middle-income countries do not differentiate between individuals starting ART for the first time and those restarting treatment, providing NNRTI-based first-line regimens regardless of prior ART exposure. The guidelines also define alternative non-NNRTI-containing first-line regimens for adults and subpopulations, including children, pregnant women, and individuals with HIV-tuberculosis (TB) coinfection. For adults, the preferred first-line ART regimen includes tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF), lamivudine (3TC) or emtricitabine (FTC), and efavirenz (EFV) as a fixed-dose combination. For adolescents aged 10–19 years, the same regimen is recommended, albeit with lower certainty of evidence. Pregnant women are also advised to use this regimen, with moderate certainty of evidence supporting its efficacy. For children aged 3–10 years, the preferred regimen includes abacavir (ABC) and lamivudine (3TC), combined with EFV. For children under three years, the recommended regimen includes ABC (or zidovudine (AZT)), 3TC, and boosted lopinavir (LPV/r). Alternative regimens for adults and adolescents include TDF, 3TC or FTC, and dolutegravir (DTG), with conditional recommendations based on moderate certainty of evidence. Regimens containing co-formulated PI/r, such as boosted atazanavir (ATV/r), LPV/r, and darunavir (DRV/r), are alternative options in specific circumstances. For pregnant women, PI/r-based regimens (ATV/r, LPV/r, or DRV/r) are recommended. For individuals with HIV-associated TB infection, dose adjustments are required for DTG, LPV/r, and raltegravir (RAL) during TB treatment with rifampicin. However, due to significant interactions with rifampicin, ATV and DRV cannot be used. For children aged 3–9 years, the alternative first-line regimen remains ABC (or AZT), 3TC, and LPV/r. For children under three years unable to tolerate an LPV/r-based regimen, the alternative regimen includes ABC (or AZT), 3TC, and RAL. The guidelines emphasize a public health approach, considering feasibility and effectiveness across diverse settings. Key principles such as availability, affordability, acceptability, accessibility, and quality were considered in developing these recommendations. The guidelines also endorse a people-centered approach to HIV treatment and care, focusing on the health needs, preferences, and expectations of individuals and communities while upholding dignity, equity, respect, and autonomy. In response to the increasing prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs in lowand middle-income countries, WHO convened a guideline development process from November 2016 to April 2017. This process involved three groups: the WHO Steering Group, the independent Guideline Development Group, and the External Review Group. These groups included geographically and gender-balanced external experts, academics, researchers, program managers, implementers, and representatives of community networks and organizations. All contributors completed a WHO declaration of interests form, and no significant conflicts of interest were identified. Recommendations were made using the GRADE (Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development, and Evaluation) approach to evidence review. Modeling, expert consultations, and country case studies informed the guidelines, identifying knowledge gaps to guide future HIVDR research. A consensus statement was formulated to indicate the threshold for pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs that should trigger a public health response. Countries with a prevalence of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs among first-line ART initiators equal to or above 10% should urgently consider transitioning to a non-NNRTI-containing first-line ART regimen. The guidelines prioritize people at greater risk of pretreatment HIVDR to NNRTIs, such as those with prior NNRTI exposure, for initiating non-NNRTI-containing regimens without requiring pretreatment HIVDR testing. Fixed-dose combinations and age-appropriate ARV formulations are recommended to maximize adherence and minimize HIVDR selection. Expanding viral load monitoring capacity and ensuring prompt switching to second-line ART in cases of virological failure are also emphasized. Strengthening treatment literacy, adherence support, and retention in care is critical to minimizing loss to follow-up and ensuring effective program implementation.
